doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Growing up in Endicott and learning drums
title: Country and Irish music at home; finding jazz on the radio
summary: Her mother played country and Irish music; she stumbled on jazz radio, hearing Booker Ervin, and says nobody really chooses jazz as a career.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Isn’t that interesting where your musical genes come from.
Hey I don’t know. I mean I really grew up in a country & western household. That’s all my mom listens to.

She likes Irish folk music too. Her family, there are a lot of Irish relatives. I like that also. But every single morning we woke up and one of those two styles of music was blaring through the house. I just remember also being a kid and spinning the dial on my radio in bed one night, I couldn’t sleep, and I accidentally twirled down to WSKG public radio in Binghamton. And I remember the song it was a Booker Ervin’s version of “The Lamp is Low.” And I heard that and I was like what is that. And it was jazz. And I didn’t know what it was and I really, really liked it. So that was an accident too. I mean my mother wouldn’t have known like where to even look for a jazz radio station. You know, it wasn’t her interest. So I found that by accident, you know along with learning the different instruments, would be bugging my teachers and they gave me a lot of recordings and so I just automatically loved it. I think everybody does that goes into jazz. I don’t think it’s a study or like really even a choice. I really don’t think it’s a choice.
I think you’re right. I think, one fella described it as an illness.

Yeah. I mean you’d be insane to pick it as an art field or a career. And parents sometimes, like at parent-teacher days or career day at college, you know, “excuse me, what’s the starting salary for a jazz musician?” And you just have to say, “uh m’am, there’s a great benefit package with that.”
Yeah. That’s like an oxymoron, a starting salary for a jazz musician I guess.
